q: What is linear regression?
short: A supervised model that predicts a continuous target as a weighted sum of features plus a bias, ŷ = wᵀx + w₀, fitted by minimising squared error.
detail: Linear in the parameters; can use non-linear features. Solved in closed form or by gradient descent.
example: Salary = w₀ + w₁ × years of experience.
mistakes: Saying it can only fit straight lines.

q: How is linear regression a neural network?
short: It is one neuron: inputs times weights summed with a bias, passed through the identity activation f(z) = z.
detail: Same forward/loss/backward/update loop as deep nets; with sigmoid it becomes logistic regression.
mistakes: Adding a sigmoid for a regression target.

q: Why use squared error?
short: It's differentiable, convex for linear models (one global minimum), penalises large errors more, and equals maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise.
detail: Downside: outlier sensitivity; MAE/Huber are alternatives.
mistakes: Claiming squared error is robust to outliers.

q: What is the gradient of the MSE loss for linear regression?
short: ∇J = (1/N)Xᵀ(Xw − y): the average of error × input.
detail: Chain rule with f′ = 1; zero gradient gives the normal equations.
mistakes: Forgetting the transpose or the 1/N.

q: What does the learning rate do?
short: Sets the gradient-descent step size: too small is slow, too large overshoots and can diverge.
detail: For a quadratic loss, stable iff η < 2/λ_max(XᵀX/N).
mistakes: Assuming larger always means faster.

q: MSE vs RMSE vs MAE?
short: MSE: average squared error (penalises big errors, squared units). RMSE: its square root (target units). MAE: average absolute error (robust, interpretable).
detail: Use MAE when outliers shouldn't dominate; RMSE when big misses are costly.
example: RMSE $24K vs MAE $19K on house prices.
mistakes: Comparing MSE across differently scaled targets.

q: What does R² measure?
short: The fraction of target variance explained: 1 − SS_res/SS_tot. 1 is perfect, 0 equals predicting the mean, negative is worse.
detail: Can be negative on test data.
example: Slides' example at the optimum: R² ≈ 0.964.
mistakes: Thinking R² can't be negative.

q: Why split data into train and test sets?
short: Training error measures fit; only error on unseen data measures generalisation.
detail: Use a validation set for tuning so the test set stays unbiased.
mistakes: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set.

q: Why scale features before gradient descent?
short: Different scales make the loss surface a long narrow valley; one η is too large for some directions and too small for others. Scaling reduces the condition number.
detail: Min–max or standardisation, statistics from the training set only.
follow: Does scaling change the closed-form solution?
mistakes: Fitting the scaler on all data.

q: Your loss turns into NaN after a few iterations. What do you check?
short: Learning rate too large, unscaled features causing overflow. Lower η, standardise, check the update sign.
detail: Plot loss per iteration; gradient-check.
example: Raw sq ft features with η = 1e-6 diverged in ex2.
follow: And if the loss doesn't move?
mistakes: Training longer.

q: Derive ∇J for J(w) = (1/2N)‖Xw − y‖².
short: J = (1/2N)(wᵀXᵀXw − 2yᵀXw + yᵀy) ⇒ ∇J = (1/2N)(2XᵀXw − 2Xᵀy) = (1/N)Xᵀ(Xw − y).
detail: Per example: ∂ℓ/∂w_j = (ŷ − y)·f′(z)·x_j = (ŷ − y)x_j.
mistakes: Sign errors in the cross term.

detail: Predictions become (1.20, 2.03, 2.87).
mistakes: Forgetting the bias column.

q: When does gradient descent on a quadratic loss converge?
short: Iff 0 < η < 2/λ_max of the Hessian (1/N)XᵀX; the speed depends on the condition number λ_max/λ_min.
detail: Error evolves as (I − ηH)ᵗ.
example: λ_max = 5.55 → η < 0.36 for the slides' data.
mistakes: Ignoring λ_min.

q: Normal equation vs gradient descent?
short: Normal equation: exact, no η, O(Nd² + d³), needs XᵀX invertible. GD: O(Nd) per step, scales to large d and streaming data, extends to non-linear models.
detail: Use solvers (QR, lstsq) rather than explicit inverses.
mistakes: Computing (XᵀX)⁻¹ explicitly for ill-conditioned data.

q: Which stopping criteria would you use?
short: Gradient norm below ε, loss change below ε, maximum iterations, or validation loss rising (early stopping).
detail: Combine a tolerance with an iteration cap.
mistakes: Only a fixed iteration count with no monitoring.

q: Training loss decreases very slowly. Diagnose.
short: η too small, poorly scaled features (ill-conditioning), or a gradient bug. Increase η, standardise, gradient-check.
detail: Plot loss on a log scale; compare analytic and numerical gradients.
example: Raw features with η = 1e-7: J = 502 after 2,000 steps vs 335 optimum.
mistakes: Assuming more epochs will fix it.

q: Why is zero initialisation fine here but not in deep nets?
short: A single neuron's loss is convex and has no hidden-unit symmetry. In multi-layer nets zero weights make all hidden units identical forever.
detail: Deep nets use random (Xavier/He) initialisation (Module 11).
mistakes: Zero-initialising hidden layers.

q: Write a vectorised GD loop for linear regression.
short: for t in range(T): g = X.T @ (X @ w - y) / N; w -= eta * g; break if norm(g) < eps.
detail: X includes the column of ones; O(Nd) per iteration.
mistakes: Looping over examples in Python instead of vectorising.

q: Show that minimising squared error is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise.
short: With y = wᵀx + ε, ε ~ N(0, σ²): −log p(y|X, w) = (1/2σ²)‖Xw − y‖² + const, so maximising likelihood = minimising squared error.
detail: Laplace noise gives MAE instead.
follow: What does a Gaussian prior on w give?
mistakes: Forgetting the i.i.d. assumption.

q: How does the condition number affect GD, and how do you fix it?
short: Iterations scale roughly with κ = λ_max/λ_min of XᵀX; large κ means zig-zagging. Fix with feature scaling/whitening, momentum, adaptive optimisers or second-order methods.
detail: Standardisation cut κ from 4.6×10⁷ to 12.6 in ex2.
follow: What does Adam do about it?
mistakes: Blaming slow convergence only on η.

q: R² is 0.95 on train and −0.2 on test. What happened?
short: Severe overfitting or a distribution shift/leakage bug; negative test R² means worse than predicting the mean.
detail: Check split, feature leakage, extrapolation; regularise, reduce features, cross-validate.
example: Time series split randomly instead of chronologically.
mistakes: Reporting train R².

q: What happens with perfectly collinear features?
short: XᵀX is singular: infinitely many minimisers; GD from zero converges to the minimum-norm solution, the normal equation fails without a pseudo-inverse or ridge penalty.
detail: Weights become uninterpretable.
example: Size in sq ft and in m² both included.
mistakes: Interpreting individual weights under collinearity.

q: Batch GD vs SGD for linear regression on 100M rows?
short: Batch GD needs a full pass per step (slow, memory-heavy); mini-batch SGD makes many cheap noisy steps and streams data.
detail: Use a decaying η or averaging for convergence; the closed form is impractical at that scale.
follow: Why must η decay for SGD?
mistakes: Loading all data into memory for each step.

q: A regression model's residuals grow with the predicted value. What does it mean and what do you do?
short: Heteroscedasticity: squared error over-weights large targets. Transform the target (log), use weighted least squares or a relative-error loss.
detail: Check residual plots, not just RMSE.
follow: How do you invert a log-target prediction?
mistakes: Ignoring residual diagnostics.
